title: Glioma
text: A glioma is a tumour that starts in the glial cells, the support cells of the brain and spinal cord. Gliomas range from slow-growing (low grade) to fast-growing (high grade, such as glioblastoma). Symptoms depend on location and can include headaches, seizures, changes in personality, weakness or trouble speaking. Diagnosis needs a specialist review of MRI with contrast and usually a biopsy to confirm the type and grade. Treatment may involve surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy, planned by a neuro-oncology team.

title: Meningioma
text: A meningioma is a tumour that grows from the meninges, the thin membranes that line and wrap the brain and spinal cord (the lining of the brain). Most meningiomas are benign (not cancer) and grow slowly; many are found by chance and only need to be watched with repeat scans. Larger ones can press on the brain and cause headaches, vision changes, seizures or weakness. A neurosurgeon decides whether to observe, operate or use radiation.

title: Pituitary tumour (adenoma)
text: A pituitary tumour grows in the pituitary gland, a pea-sized gland at the base of the brain that controls many hormones. Almost all are non-cancerous adenomas. They can cause problems by producing too much of a hormone or by pressing on nearby nerves, especially the nerves for vision. Doctors check hormone blood tests and vision fields along with MRI. Treatment can be medicine, surgery or simply monitoring.

title: No tumour pattern on MRI
text: When the classifier does not find a tumour pattern, it means the image does not match the glioma, meningioma or pituitary examples it learned from. It does not rule out other brain conditions such as stroke, infection, multiple sclerosis or very small lesions. Only a radiologist's report can say whether a scan is normal.

title: Brain MRI scan
text: A brain MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves to make detailed pictures of the brain without X-ray radiation. Different sequences (T1, T2, FLAIR) highlight different tissues, and contrast dye (gadolinium) can show areas where the blood-brain barrier is disrupted, which helps detect tumours and inflammation. A radiologist reads the full set of images, not a single slice.

title: Grad-CAM heatmap
text: Grad-CAM is an explainability method that colours the regions of an image that most influenced a neural network's prediction. Warm colours show the areas the model relied on. A heatmap shows where the model looked, not proof that disease is present there; it helps a clinician judge whether the model focused on a sensible region.

title: Warning signs of brain tumours
text: Possible warning signs include new headaches that are worse in the morning or with coughing, new seizures, progressive weakness or numbness on one side, changes in vision, speech or personality, and persistent nausea. Sudden severe symptoms such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech need emergency care because they can also signal a stroke.

title: Anaemia
text: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin or too few red cells to carry enough oxygen. Common causes are iron deficiency, low vitamin B12 or folate, blood loss, and long-term illness. Symptoms include tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and dizziness. Doctors look at haemoglobin together with MCV, ferritin and B12 to find the cause before treating it.

title: Prediabetes and diabetes
text: Prediabetes means blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet in the diabetes range: fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%. Diabetes is usually diagnosed with fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more, or HbA1c of 6.5% or more, confirmed on repeat testing. Regular activity, weight management and a balanced diet can slow or stop progression.

title: Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
text: Hypothyroidism means the thyroid makes too little hormone. The typical blood pattern is a high TSH with low or normal T4. It can cause tiredness, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, feeling cold and low mood. It is common, especially in women, and is usually managed with daily thyroid hormone replacement prescribed by a doctor.

title: Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
text: Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid makes too much hormone. The typical blood pattern is a low TSH with high T3 or T4. It can cause a fast heartbeat, weight loss, anxiety, tremor and heat intolerance. Doctors find the cause with further tests before choosing treatment.

title: Raised liver enzymes and fatty liver
text: Mildly raised ALT and AST are often caused by fat building up in the liver, which is linked with excess weight, diabetes and alcohol. Other causes include viral hepatitis and some medicines. Doctors may repeat the test, ask about alcohol and medicines and order an ultrasound. Weight loss and less alcohol often bring the enzymes back down.

title: Kidney function results
text: Creatinine, urea and eGFR together show how well the kidneys filter the blood. One raised result can be due to dehydration or a high-protein meal, so doctors usually repeat it. An eGFR below 60 lasting three months or more suggests chronic kidney disease. Blood pressure and blood sugar control protect the kidneys.

title: Dehydration in blood tests
text: When the body is short of water, the blood becomes more concentrated. This can make haemoglobin, haematocrit, sodium, urea and albumin read higher than usual. Results often return to normal after drinking enough fluids and repeating the test.

title: Inflammation markers
text: ESR and CRP are general signs of inflammation. They rise with infections, autoimmune conditions and injuries, but they do not show the cause or location. Doctors interpret them together with symptoms and other results.

title: Low platelets during fever
text: Platelet counts often fall during viral fevers, and in India dengue is a common cause. Warning signs that need urgent care include bleeding gums or nose, black stools, severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting or extreme weakness. Doctors track platelets daily during dengue.

title: Vitamin D deficiency
text: Vitamin D deficiency is very common in India despite sunshine, because of indoor lifestyles and covered skin. Levels below 20 ng/mL are usually called deficient and 20–29 insufficient. Low levels can cause bone and muscle aches. A doctor decides the right supplement and dose.

title: Vitamin B12 deficiency
text: B12 is found mostly in animal foods, so vegetarians and vegans are at higher risk of deficiency. Low B12 can cause anaemia with large red cells (high MCV), tiredness, tingling in hands and feet and memory problems. It is treated with supplements or injections prescribed by a doctor.

title: Cholesterol and heart health
text: High LDL and triglycerides and low HDL raise the long-term risk of heart attack and stroke. Doctors judge the overall risk using age, blood pressure, diabetes, smoking and family history, not cholesterol alone. Eating more fibre and less fried food, exercising and not smoking all help; some people also need medicine.

title: High uric acid and gout
text: When uric acid is high, crystals can form in joints and cause sudden painful swelling called gout, often in the big toe. Many people with high uric acid never get gout. Red meat, seafood, alcohol and sugary drinks can raise levels.

title: Jaundice and bilirubin
text: Jaundice is yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by high bilirubin. It can come from liver inflammation (for example hepatitis), blocked bile ducts or rapid breakdown of red cells. New jaundice should always be checked by a doctor.

title: What a reference range means
text: A reference range is the span of values seen in about 95% of healthy people. This means a few healthy people fall slightly outside it. Ranges differ between laboratories, ages and sexes, so the range printed on your own report is the one to compare against. One result slightly outside the range is often not significant on its own.

title: Critical lab values
text: Some results are far enough from normal that they may need same-day medical attention, for example very low haemoglobin, very high or low potassium or sodium, or very low platelets. Laboratories usually phone the doctor about these. If your report shows a value marked critical, contact your doctor promptly.

title: Electrolytes
text: Electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, chloride and calcium are minerals that carry electrical charges and control fluid balance, nerve signals, muscle contraction and heart rhythm. Vomiting, diarrhoea, kidney problems and some medicines like water pills can change them.
